title: Need a skilled interpreter, not an infallible one — sense has light in the text itself
source_text: XLIV. Itaque ut fideles verum Scripturae sensum in multis assequantur, & uberem fructum ex ea capiant, opus habent quidem interprete, sed non interprete qui errare non possit, ut dicunt Pontificii, verum interprete sagaci & perito. At, postquam illis praeivit ejusmodi interpres, Scripturae sensum tenent, & de eo certi sunt, non propter authoritatem, sive interpretis, sive traditionis, quam ex interprete suo didicerunt: sed propter vim & lucem veritatis, quam jam in rebus ipsis agnoscunt & animadvertunt, si quidem mentem, ut decet, Spiritus sancti virtute purgatam, & illuminatam habeant. Quemadmodum qui student Philosophiae & literis humanioribus per se statim non possunt intelligere textum Aristotelis, & Horatii vel Juvenalis Satyras, sed ad opera praeceptoris & magistri. Et tamen postquam verus, vel Poetae, vel Philosophi sensus ipsis indicatus & expositus est, illum jam proprio judicio discernunt & vident in ipso authore: Nec de eo persuasi sunt propter solam magistri sui authoritatem. Etenim sicut sensus Poematum Horatii & Aristotelici textus ex se incertus & dubius non est, donec accedat aliqua externa authoritas, quae super eo pronunciet, sed ex ipsis authorum verbis atque operum contextura certo deprehendi potest, modo debite expendantur: ita quoque verus Scripturae sacrae sensus habet in ipso textu propriam lucem, & sui argumenta atque probationes quibus innotescere possit, nec est per se vagus & indeterminatus donec accedat authoritas traditionis non scriptae, vel judicii Ecclesiastici quae illum certo modo limitet & coarctet.
pass_a_gloss: Therefore that the faithful may attain the true sense of Scripture in many things, and take rich fruit from it, they indeed have need of an interpreter, but not of an interpreter who cannot err, as the Pontificians say, but of a sagacious and skilled interpreter. But, after such an interpreter has gone before them, they hold the sense of Scripture, and are certain of it, not on account of the authority either of the interpreter or of the tradition which they learned from their interpreter: but on account of the force and light of truth, which they now acknowledge and notice in the things themselves, if indeed they have a mind, as is fitting, purged and illuminated by the power of the Holy Spirit. Just as those who study Philosophy and the more humane letters cannot at once by themselves understand the text of Aristotle, and the Satires of Horace or Juvenal, but need the work of a teacher and master. And yet after the true sense of the Poet or Philosopher has been indicated and expounded to them, they already discern it by their own judgment and see it in the author himself: Nor are they persuaded of it on account of the sole authority of their master. For just as the sense of Horace's Poems and of the Aristotelian text is not of itself uncertain and doubtful until some external authority come in which pronounces upon it, but can be certainly detected from the very words of the authors and the texture of the works, provided they be duly weighed: so also the true sense of sacred Scripture has in the text itself its own light, and its arguments and proofs by which it can become known, nor is it of itself vague and indeterminate until the authority of unwritten tradition, or of Ecclesiastical judgment, come in which limits and constrains it in a certain way.
pass_b_english: Faithful readers need a skilled interpreter — not Rome's interpreter who cannot err.
After guidance, certainty rests on the light of truth in the things themselves under the Spirit, not on the guide's or tradition's authority.
Like Aristotle or Horace: a teacher helps, but then you see the sense in the author by your own judgment.
Scripture's sense has light and proofs in the text; it is not blank until tradition or Church judgment fences it.
